---
title: "Quiz: meshes, coordinate spaces and projection"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Conventions: the camera looks down $-z$ in view space; after the divide by $w$, everything visible lies in the cube $[-1, 1]^3$.

---

**Q1.** Why does an indexed triangle list need less memory than storing three positions per triangle?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many triangles share a vertex in a closed mesh?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each vertex of a closed mesh is shared by about six triangles. Indexed, its position (12 bytes) is stored once and each triangle stores three 4-byte indices; as a soup it is stored about six times. For $10^6$ triangles: about 18 MB indexed against 36 MB as a soup.
:::

---

**Q2.** Two neighbouring triangles of a mesh both list their shared edge as "vertex 5, then vertex 7". What is wrong, and what will you see?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Winding decides which side is the front.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
In a consistently oriented mesh the two triangles traverse the shared edge in opposite directions. Here one of them is wound the other way: its normal points inwards. With back-face culling it disappears (a hole), and its lighting is wrong.
:::

---

**Q3.** Why does a direction such as a normal or a light direction get $w = 0$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens to the translation column of a $4\times4$ matrix?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The translation column is multiplied by $w$. With $w = 0$ it has no effect: moving an object does not change which way a direction points. Rotations and scales still act on it.
:::

---

**Q4.** You want to turn a house about its own centre and then place it at $(5, 0, 0)$. Is the model matrix $TR$ or $RT$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The matrix next to the vector acts first.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$TR$: $R$ turns the house about the origin of model space (its centre), then $T$ moves it. $RT$ would first move it to $(5, 0, 0)$ and then swing it around the world origin.
:::

---

**Q5.** The camera moves 1 unit to the left. What happens to the view-space coordinates of every object?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$V$ is the inverse of the camera's placement.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
They all move 1 unit to the right ($x$ increases by 1). The view matrix undoes the camera's placement, so moving the camera one way is the same as moving the world the other way.
:::

---

**Q6.** Why can the perspective projection not be done by a $4\times4$ matrix alone, and how is it done?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$x_s = n x/(-z)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Dividing by $z$ is not linear, and a matrix product is linear in the coordinates. The matrix copies $-z$ into the fourth coordinate $w$; the hardware then divides $x$, $y$ and $z$ by $w$ (the perspective divide).
:::

---

**Q7.** With $n = 1$ and $f = 3$, a point halfway between the near and far planes gets the NDC depth 0.5, not 0. Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
After the divide, depth is $A + B/z$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Depth after the divide is a function of $1/z$, not of $z$: it changes fast near the camera and slowly far away. With $z_\text{ndc} = 2 + 3/z$, the point at $z = -2$ gets $2 - 1.5 = 0.5$. Three quarters of the depth range is spent on the nearer half of the distances.
:::

---

**Q8.** In an orthographic view, does an object get smaller when it moves away from the camera? Name a use in image analysis.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is $w$ after an orthographic projection?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No: $w = 1$, so there is no division by distance; parallel lines stay parallel. Microscopy viewers and maximum-intensity projections are usually orthographic, so that lengths in the image can be compared and measured.
:::

---

**Q9.** A vertex has clip coordinates $(0.4, 0.2, -2, -0.5)$. Is it visible? What would happen if it were divided by $w$ right away?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Inside the frustum means $-w \le x, y, z \le w$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$w < 0$: the vertex is behind the camera, so it is not visible. Dividing gives $(-0.8, -0.4, 4)$: the signs flip and the point would appear on the opposite side of the screen. Triangles are clipped against the near plane in clip space, before the divide.
:::

---

**Q10.** One camera sees a bright spot at a pixel. Can you tell from this one image how far away the spot is?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Run the pipeline backwards from a pixel.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. A pixel corresponds to a whole ray from the eye; every point on that ray projects to the same pixel. A second camera at another position gives a second ray, and the spot lies where the two rays meet (stereo).
:::
